• Amazon Textract: Textract extracts text from documents.

Key takeaway: Image and video moderation → Amazon Rekognition.

stem: A company wants to detect bias in its training data and model predictions across demographic groups. Which AWS capability fits?

choices.text: Amazon SageMaker Debugger
Amazon SageMaker Studio Lab
Amazon SageMaker Neo
Amazon SageMaker Clarify

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Clarify measures bias in data and predictions and provides feature attributions for explainability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SageMaker Debugger: Debugger monitors training jobs for issues such as vanishing gradients.
• Amazon SageMaker Studio Lab: Studio Lab is a free learning environment.
• Amazon SageMaker Neo: Neo optimizes models for hardware.

Key takeaway: Bias detection and explainability → SageMaker Clarify.

stem: A generative AI app must block hateful and violent content in both user prompts and model responses. Which AWS feature fits?

choices.text: Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput
Amazon Bedrock model customization
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails content filters
Amazon Bedrock batch inference jobs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Guardrails content filters detect and block harmful categories such as hate and violence in inputs and outputs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput: Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity.
• Amazon Bedrock model customization: Customization adapts models but is not a runtime filter.
• Amazon Bedrock batch inference jobs: Batch inference processes offline jobs.

Key takeaway: Filter harmful content with Bedrock Guardrails.

stem: A loan model was trained on data where one group is heavily underrepresented. Which responsible AI concern arises most directly?

choices.text: The model will train faster because it has fewer records
The model may perform worse or unfairly for that group
The model will automatically correct the imbalance itself
The model cannot be deployed to any AWS Region at all

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Underrepresented groups often receive less accurate or biased predictions; rebalancing data and measuring outcomes by group help.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The model will train faster because it has…: Training speed is not the concern.
• The model will automatically correct the…: Models do not self-correct imbalance.
• The model cannot be deployed to any AWS…: Deployment is not blocked by imbalance.

Key takeaway: Underrepresentation can cause unfair model behavior.

stem: A human review step is needed for low-confidence predictions from an ML model before decisions are made. Which AWS service supports this workflow?

choices.text: Amazon Augmented AI (A2I)
Amazon CloudWatch Logs
Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS)
AWS Step Functions Express workflows

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon A2I adds human review workflows for ML predictions, such as routing low-confidence results to reviewers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon CloudWatch Logs: CloudWatch Logs stores logs.
• Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS): SNS sends notifications.
• AWS Step Functions Express workflows: Step Functions orchestrates but does not provide review workflows by itself.

Key takeaway: Human review of ML predictions → Amazon A2I.

stem: A company explains to customers which factors most influenced an individual loan decision. Which responsible AI concept does this represent?

choices.text: Explainability
Portability
Robustness
Scalability

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Explaining the factors behind an individual decision is explainability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Portability: Portability is moving models between environments.
• Robustness: Robustness is stability under varied inputs.
• Scalability: Scalability is handling more load.

Key takeaway: Reasons for individual decisions = explainability.

stem: A company needs to explain which features drove a tabular model's predictions. Which technique does SageMaker Clarify use for feature attributions?

choices.text: Dropout layers
Gradient boosting
SHAP values
K-means clustering

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clarify uses SHAP (Shapley values) to attribute how much each feature contributed to predictions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dropout layers: Dropout is a training regularization method.
• Gradient boosting: Gradient boosting is a modeling algorithm.
• K-means clustering: K-means is clustering.

Key takeaway: Feature attributions in Clarify use SHAP.

stem: A healthcare company must choose between an interpretable model with slightly lower accuracy and a complex model with slightly higher accuracy. Clinicians must understand each recommendation. Which choice fits?

choices.text: The complex model, with explanations invented later by the support team
The complex model, since the highest accuracy always outweighs interpretability
Neither, since no model can ever be used for any healthcare recommendation
The interpretable model, since understanding each recommendation is required

explanation:
Why this is correct:
When understanding recommendations is required and the accuracy gap is small, interpretability should take priority.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The complex model, with explanations…: Invented explanations are not real explanations.
• The complex model, since the highest…: Accuracy is not always decisive.
• Neither, since no model can ever be used for…: Models can be used responsibly with oversight.

Key takeaway: Prefer interpretable models when explanations are required and accuracy costs are small.

stem: A company wants to disclose to users that its chatbot responses are generated by AI. Which principle does this support?

choices.text: Resilience
Transparency
Veracity
Efficiency

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Disclosing AI involvement helps users understand what they are interacting with, which is transparency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Resilience: Resilience concerns recovery from failures.
• Veracity: Veracity concerns accuracy of outputs.
• Efficiency: Efficiency concerns resource use.

Key takeaway: Disclosing AI use = transparency.

stem: Which TWO actions reduce the environmental impact of generative AI workloads? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Choose the smallest model that meets quality needs
Run duplicate inference on every request for safety
Always pick the largest model to minimize retries
Retrain the model from scratch for every small update
Use energy-efficient accelerators such as AWS Inferentia

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Right-sizing models and using efficient hardware reduce energy use per task.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Run duplicate inference on every request for…: Duplicate inference doubles consumption.
• Always pick the largest model to minimize…: Larger models use more energy.
• Retrain the model from scratch for every…: Unnecessary retraining wastes energy.

Key takeaway: Right-size models and use efficient hardware for sustainability.

stem: A generative AI tool produces text that closely copies copyrighted articles. Which responsible AI risk is this?

choices.text: Insufficient compute for peak demand
Excessive inference latency for users
Intellectual property infringement
Model underfitting on training data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reproducing protected content creates intellectual property risk; controls include review, filtering, and usage policies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Insufficient compute for peak demand: Compute capacity is an infrastructure issue.
• Excessive inference latency for users: Latency is a performance issue.
• Model underfitting on training data: Underfitting is a training issue.

Key takeaway: Reproducing protected content is an IP risk.

stem: A company wants to document a model's intended uses, limitations, and evaluation results for transparency. Which AWS feature fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Ground Truth
SageMaker Model Cards
SageMaker Autopilot
SageMaker Edge Manager

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model Cards record intended uses, limitations, risk ratings, and evaluation details.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SageMaker Ground Truth: Ground Truth labels data.
• SageMaker Autopilot: Autopilot builds models automatically.
• SageMaker Edge Manager: Edge Manager manages edge deployments.

Key takeaway: Transparency documentation → SageMaker Model Cards.

stem: Which TWO characteristics describe a responsible dataset for training a model that serves diverse customers? (Select TWO)

choices.text: It excludes all minority groups to simplify training
It contains as many duplicate records as possible
It comes only from the most convenient data source
It is collected with appropriate consent and rights
It represents the groups the model will serve

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Responsible datasets are representative of users and lawfully and ethically sourced.

Why the other options are wrong:
• It excludes all minority groups to simplify…: Excluding groups causes unfair outcomes.
• It contains as many duplicate records as…: Duplicates distort learning.
• It comes only from the most convenient data…: Convenience sampling often introduces bias.

Key takeaway: Responsible data is representative and properly sourced.

stem: A regulator asks a bank to show why its model denied a specific applicant. Which approach meets this need best?

choices.text: Provide per-prediction feature attributions and the model's documentation
Provide the model's source code files without any further explanation
Provide a statement that the vendor guarantees the model is fair
Provide the total number of loans the model approved last quarter

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Per-prediction attributions explain an individual decision, and documentation provides context on the model's design and limits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Provide the model's source code files…: Source code alone does not explain a specific decision.
• Provide a statement that the vendor…: Vendor guarantees are not explanations.
• Provide the total number of loans the model…: Aggregate counts do not explain one decision.

Key takeaway: Explain individual decisions with attributions plus documentation.

stem: A team says its model should work reliably even when inputs are noisy or slightly unusual. Which responsible AI dimension is this?

choices.text: Fairness
Controllability
Robustness
Privacy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Robustness means the system behaves reliably under varied, noisy, or unexpected inputs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fairness: Fairness concerns equitable treatment.
• Controllability: Controllability concerns human ability to steer or stop the system.
• Privacy: Privacy concerns protecting personal data.

Key takeaway: Reliable behavior under unusual inputs = robustness.

stem: Which statement correctly contrasts transparent (interpretable) models with black-box models?

choices.text: Black-box models cannot be deployed on AWS, while interpretable models can be
Interpretable models show how inputs lead to outputs; black-box models are harder to explain
Interpretable models are always more accurate than black-box models on every task
Interpretable models require no data, while black-box models require training data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Interpretable models, such as linear models or small trees, show their reasoning; complex models often need separate explanation methods.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Black-box models cannot be deployed on AWS,…: Both can be deployed on AWS.
• Interpretable models are always more…: Interpretable models are not always more accurate.
• Interpretable models require no data, while…: Both require data.

Key takeaway: Interpretability is a trade-off with complexity, not a guarantee of accuracy.

stem: A startup wants to prototype a generative AI feature quickly and pay only for what it uses, without managing servers. Which advantage of managed foundation model services applies most?

choices.text: Guaranteed zero hallucinations for every response the models generate
Unlimited free usage for the first year of production traffic volume
Complete ownership of the model weights for resale to other companies
Fast time to market with pay-per-use pricing and no infrastructure to run

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Managed services such as Amazon Bedrock let teams start quickly, pay per use, and avoid managing infrastructure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Guaranteed zero hallucinations for every…: No service guarantees zero hallucinations.
• Unlimited free usage for the first year of…: There is no unlimited free production usage.
• Complete ownership of the model weights for…: Managed models are accessed, not owned for resale.

Key takeaway: Managed GenAI = speed, pay-per-use, no infrastructure.

stem: A company wants to use generative AI for customer-facing medical advice. Which limitation is the most serious concern?

choices.text: The model can produce plausible but incorrect advice that harms users
The model requires customers to install special desktop software
The model responds too slowly for most patients using mobile devices
The model cannot produce text in any language other than English

explanation:
Why this is correct:
In high-stakes domains, confident but wrong outputs can cause harm; human oversight, grounding, and scope limits are essential.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The model requires customers to install…: No special software is required.
• The model responds too slowly for most…: Latency is manageable and not the main risk.
• The model cannot produce text in any…: Many models support multiple languages.

Key takeaway: In high-stakes domains, inaccurate outputs are the core risk.

stem: Which statement describes a key difference between generative AI and traditional predictive ML?

choices.text: Predictive ML can only run on premises, while generative AI runs in the cloud
Generative AI creates new content; predictive ML outputs labels or values
Generative AI needs no data, while predictive ML always needs labeled data
Generative AI is always deterministic, while predictive ML is always random

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Generative models produce new content such as text or images; predictive models output classes, scores, or numbers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Predictive ML can only run on premises,…: Both run in either environment.
• Generative AI needs no data, while…: Generative models are trained on large amounts of data.
• Generative AI is always deterministic, while…: Generative AI is typically non-deterministic.

Key takeaway: Generative AI produces content; predictive ML produces predictions.

stem: A company compares a very large foundation model and a smaller one for a simple FAQ assistant. Both meet accuracy needs. Which factors favor the smaller model?

choices.text: Automatic compliance with all data regulations
Guaranteed immunity to prompt injection attacks
Lower cost per request and lower response latency
Better performance on every possible reasoning task

explanation:
Why this is correct:
When quality needs are met, smaller models usually cost less and respond faster.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic compliance with all data regulations: Compliance depends on how the system is built and governed.
• Guaranteed immunity to prompt injection attacks: No model is immune to prompt injection.
• Better performance on every possible…: Smaller models are not better on every task.

Key takeaway: If quality is sufficient, prefer smaller models for cost and speed.

stem: Which TWO are common limitations of foundation models that businesses should plan for? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Inability to process more than one word at a time
Requirement to be retrained before every request
Guaranteed bias in every single response they give
Knowledge that stops at a training cutoff date
Outputs that can vary for the same prompt

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Models have a knowledge cutoff and can be non-deterministic; grounding and parameter tuning address these.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inability to process more than one word at a…: Models process whole sequences.
• Requirement to be retrained before every request: No retraining is needed per request.
• Guaranteed bias in every single response…: Bias risk exists but is not guaranteed in every response.

Key takeaway: Plan for knowledge cutoffs and output variability.

stem: Employees want a generative AI assistant that answers questions using content from Confluence, SharePoint, and Salesforce while respecting permissions. Which AWS service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Q Business
Amazon Q Developer
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon SageMaker Canvas

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon Q Business connects to enterprise data sources and answers questions while respecting user access permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Q Developer: Q Developer targets software development.
• Amazon Rekognition: Rekognition analyzes images and video.
• Amazon SageMaker Canvas: Canvas builds ML models without code.

Key takeaway: Enterprise knowledge assistant with permissions → Amazon Q Business.

stem: A company wants business users to get generative AI insights and summaries from their BI dashboards using natural language. Which AWS capability fits?

choices.text: Amazon Transcribe call analytics for contact centers
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for real-time ingestion
Generative BI capabilities in Amazon Quick Sight
AWS Glue ETL jobs for building data pipelines

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon Quick Sight provides generative BI features that let users ask questions and generate summaries of dashboard data in natural language.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Transcribe call analytics for contact…: Transcribe call analytics analyzes calls.
• Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for real-time…: Kinesis ingests streaming data.
• AWS Glue ETL jobs for building data pipelines: Glue builds data pipelines.

Key takeaway: Natural-language BI insights → generative BI in Quick Sight.

stem: A team needs cost-effective hardware for running inference on large generative AI models in its own endpoints on AWS. Which AWS-designed chip is built for this?

choices.text: AWS Nitro Enclaves
AWS Inferentia
AWS Outposts
AWS Graviton

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Inferentia accelerators are designed for high-performance, low-cost deep learning inference; Trainium targets training.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Nitro Enclaves: Nitro Enclaves isolate sensitive processing.
• AWS Outposts: Outposts brings AWS infrastructure on premises.
• AWS Graviton: Graviton is a general-purpose CPU.

Key takeaway: Inferentia for inference; Trainium for training.

stem: Which statement correctly compares Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker AI for generative AI?

choices.text: Bedrock requires customers to launch and manage their own GPU instances for each model they invoke
Bedrock is only for image generation models, while SageMaker AI is only for text models of any size or type
SageMaker AI cannot host foundation models of any kind, so all generative AI workloads must use Bedrock
Bedrock offers serverless access to managed models; SageMaker AI gives control to build, train, and host models

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock provides managed, serverless model access; SageMaker AI offers full control over training, tuning, and hosting, including foundation models via JumpStart.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bedrock requires customers to launch and…: Bedrock is serverless.
• Bedrock is only for image generation models,…: Both support many modalities.
• SageMaker AI cannot host foundation models…: SageMaker AI can host foundation models.

Key takeaway: Bedrock = managed and serverless; SageMaker AI = full control.

stem: A company wants to estimate monthly costs for a generative AI application before launch. Which factor most directly drives Amazon Bedrock on-demand costs?

choices.text: The number of input and output tokens processed
The number of IAM roles defined in the account
The number of Availability Zones in the Region
The number of employees with AWS console access

explanation:
Why this is correct:
On-demand pricing for text models is based on input and output tokens processed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The number of IAM roles defined in the account: IAM roles are free and unrelated.
• The number of Availability Zones in the Region: AZ count does not affect token pricing.
• The number of employees with AWS console access: Console users do not drive invocation cost.

Key takeaway: Bedrock on-demand cost = tokens in and out.

stem: A search system converts sentences into numeric vectors so that similar meanings are close together. What are these vectors called?

choices.text: Hyperparameters
Tokenizers
Embeddings
Checkpoints

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Embeddings are numeric representations that capture semantic meaning, enabling similarity search.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hyperparameters: Hyperparameters configure training.
• Tokenizers: Tokenizers split text into tokens.
• Checkpoints: Checkpoints save model state during training.

Key takeaway: Semantic vectors = embeddings.

stem: A model is described as having billions of 'parameters.' What are parameters?

choices.text: The users allowed to invoke the model within a single account
The learned weights that encode what the model learned in training
The number of documents the model can search during a request
The settings a user types into each prompt to shape a response

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Parameters are the internal weights adjusted during training; more parameters generally mean more capacity and higher cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The users allowed to invoke the model within…: User access is controlled by IAM.
• The number of documents the model can search…: Document search is retrieval.
• The settings a user types into each prompt…: Prompt settings are inference parameters, not learned weights.

Key takeaway: Parameters are learned weights; inference settings are separate.

stem: A company wants a model that can answer questions about uploaded product photos in natural language. Which model capability is required?

choices.text: Text-only generation with a longer context window
Speech synthesis with multiple voices and accents
Tabular regression over numeric product features
Multimodal input understanding of images and text

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Answering questions about images requires a multimodal model that accepts image and text inputs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Text-only generation with a longer context…: Text-only models cannot see images.
• Speech synthesis with multiple voices and…: Speech synthesis produces audio.
• Tabular regression over numeric product features: Regression predicts numbers from tables.

Key takeaway: Questions about images need multimodal models.

stem: During inference, a large language model produces text one piece at a time. How does it generate each next piece?

choices.text: It selects words randomly without considering the earlier text
It retrieves the next sentence from a stored copy of the internet
It predicts the most likely next token given all previous tokens
It translates the prompt into code and then executes that code

explanation:
Why this is correct:
LLMs generate text autoregressively, predicting the next token based on the preceding context.

Why the other options are wrong:
• It selects words randomly without…: Selection depends on context, not pure randomness.
• It retrieves the next sentence from a stored…: Models do not store and retrieve the internet.
• It translates the prompt into code and then…: Generation is not code execution.

Key takeaway: LLMs generate text by predicting the next token.

stem: Which TWO AWS services let a company use generative AI without training its own foundation model? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Amazon Q Business
Amazon EBS volumes
AWS Direct Connect
Amazon Route 53
Amazon Bedrock

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock provides access to pre-trained foundation models, and Q Business is a ready-to-use generative AI assistant.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon EBS volumes: EBS provides block storage.
• AWS Direct Connect: Direct Connect provides private network links.
• Amazon Route 53: Route 53 provides DNS.

Key takeaway: Use Bedrock or Amazon Q for ready-made generative AI.

stem: A company worries its generative AI app may give different answers to the same question over time as the provider updates the model. Which practice reduces this risk?

choices.text: Always use the newest model version without any testing
Pin a specific model version and test before upgrading
Remove logging so that changes cannot be compared later
Increase temperature so users expect varied responses

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pinning model versions and testing upgrades keeps behavior stable and lets teams evaluate changes before adopting them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Always use the newest model version without…: Untested upgrades can change behavior unexpectedly.
• Remove logging so that changes cannot be…: Without logs, changes cannot be detected.
• Increase temperature so users expect varied…: More randomness increases variation.

Key takeaway: Pin model versions and test upgrades.

stem: Which TWO statements about tokens are accurate for business planning? (Select TWO)

choices.text: One token is always exactly one full English word
Token counts do not affect response latency at all
Tokens are only counted for image generation models
Context window limits are measured in tokens
Longer prompts and responses use more tokens and cost more

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tokens drive cost and context limits; a token is often part of a word, and more tokens generally increase latency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One token is always exactly one full English…: Tokens are often subword units.
• Token counts do not affect response latency…: More tokens usually mean more processing time.
• Tokens are only counted for image generation…: Text models count tokens.

Key takeaway: Tokens drive cost, limits, and latency.

stem: A marketing team uses a foundation model to create ad copy. Which business benefit of generative AI does this best demonstrate?

choices.text: Faster content creation with more variations to test
Elimination of the need for any human marketing staff
Guaranteed legal compliance of every advertisement
Exact prediction of each campaign's final sales revenue

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Generative AI accelerates content production and makes it easy to create variations for testing, while humans still review and decide.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Elimination of the need for any human…: Humans remain essential for strategy and review.
• Guaranteed legal compliance of every…: Compliance still needs review.
• Exact prediction of each campaign's final…: Generation does not predict exact revenue.

Key takeaway: GenAI speeds up content creation and experimentation.

stem: A company must decide whether generative AI output can be used without review. Which factor matters most?

choices.text: The time of day the content is being generated
The number of words in each generated response
The consequences of an error for the people affected
The programming language used by the application

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The level of human review should match the impact of mistakes; high-impact uses need review before outputs are used.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The time of day the content is being generated: Time of day is irrelevant.
• The number of words in each generated response: Length does not determine risk.
• The programming language used by the application: Programming language is irrelevant.

Key takeaway: Match human review to the impact of errors.

stem: A company wants to generate images for product mockups using a managed model on AWS. Which option fits?

choices.text: Amazon Rekognition custom labels for classification
An image generation model available in Amazon Bedrock
Amazon Textract analysis for scanned product pages
Amazon Comprehend entity detection for descriptions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock offers image generation models, such as Amazon Nova Canvas, for creating images from prompts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Rekognition custom labels for…: Rekognition analyzes images; it does not create them.
• Amazon Textract analysis for scanned product…: Textract extracts document text.
• Amazon Comprehend entity detection for…: Comprehend analyzes text.

Key takeaway: Image generation on AWS → image models in Bedrock.

stem: A company's RAG application must retrieve documents only for the correct customer tenant. Which design feature supports this?

choices.text: A higher temperature for the text generation step
A longer system prompt describing all tenant names
A larger embedding model for every single document
Metadata filtering on retrieval by tenant identifier

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tagging chunks with metadata and filtering retrieval by tenant limits results to that tenant's documents.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A higher temperature for the text generation…: Temperature affects generation, not retrieval scope.
• A longer system prompt describing all tenant…: Prompts cannot enforce which documents are retrieved.
• A larger embedding model for every single…: Embedding size does not enforce isolation.

Key takeaway: Enforce tenant scoping with metadata filters in retrieval.

stem: A company must choose between RAG and fine-tuning for an assistant that answers about fast-changing internal policies. Which consideration decides it?

choices.text: RAG permanently changes the model weights after every user question
Fine-tuning always costs less than RAG for any amount of source data
Fine-tuning makes it impossible for the model to hallucinate facts
RAG reflects updates at query time, while fine-tuning must be repeated

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RAG retrieves current documents at query time; fine-tuned knowledge becomes stale and needs retraining.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RAG permanently changes the model weights…: RAG does not change weights.
• Fine-tuning always costs less than RAG for…: Repeated fine-tuning is often more costly.
• Fine-tuning makes it impossible for the…: Fine-tuned models can still hallucinate.

Key takeaway: Fast-changing facts favor RAG over fine-tuning.

stem: A company wants its assistant to handle long conversations while keeping costs predictable. Which design choice helps most?

choices.text: Send the entire conversation history every time
Increase max tokens for every single response
Summarize or trim older turns before sending them
Duplicate each request to two different models

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Summarizing or truncating older context reduces tokens per request, controlling cost and staying within context limits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Send the entire conversation history every time: Full history grows cost with every turn.
• Increase max tokens for every single response: Longer outputs raise cost.
• Duplicate each request to two different models: Duplicate requests double cost.

Key takeaway: Manage conversation context to control tokens and cost.

stem: A prompt includes one worked example of the desired answer format before the actual question. Which technique is this?

choices.text: One-shot prompting
Prompt chaining
Fine-tuning
Zero-shot prompting

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Including a single example is one-shot prompting; zero-shot has no examples, few-shot has several.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Prompt chaining: Prompt chaining splits a task across multiple prompts.
• Fine-tuning: Fine-tuning changes model weights.
• Zero-shot prompting: Zero-shot has no examples.

Key takeaway: Zero-shot = no examples; one-shot = one; few-shot = several.

stem: A complex report task works poorly in one prompt. The team splits it: extract facts, then analyze, then write. Which technique is this?

choices.text: Model distillation
Prompt chaining
Data augmentation
Negative prompting

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Prompt chaining breaks a complex task into sequential prompts where each step's output feeds the next.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Model distillation: Distillation trains a smaller model from a larger one.
• Data augmentation: Data augmentation expands training data.
• Negative prompting: Negative prompting specifies what to avoid, mainly in image generation.

Key takeaway: Break complex tasks into chained prompts.

stem: A company wants to store, version, and reuse approved prompts across several applications. Which Amazon Bedrock feature fits?

choices.text: Provisioned Throughput
Prompt Management
Custom model import
Model invocation logs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock Prompt Management stores, versions, and shares prompts for reuse across applications.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Provisioned Throughput: Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity.
• Custom model import: Custom model import brings in external models.
• Model invocation logs: Invocation logs record requests and responses.

Key takeaway: Store and version prompts with Bedrock Prompt Management.

stem: Which TWO elements typically improve a prompt's results? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Unrelated background text to make the prompt longer
Vague wording so the model can interpret it freely
Contradictory rules that the model must reconcile
Clear instructions describing the task and constraints
Relevant context or data the model needs to answer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clear instructions and relevant context are core prompt elements; vague, contradictory, or irrelevant content degrades results.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unrelated background text to make the prompt…: Irrelevant text adds cost and noise.
• Vague wording so the model can interpret it…: Vagueness produces inconsistent results.
• Contradictory rules that the model must…: Contradictions confuse the model.

Key takeaway: Good prompts give clear instructions and relevant context.

stem: A company wants to adapt a Bedrock model to its domain but has only a small labeled dataset. What should it try first?

choices.text: Training a new foundation model from scratch
Deleting the labeled data and using defaults
Prompt engineering and RAG before any fine-tuning
Continued pre-training on the small labeled set

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Prompting and retrieval are cheaper and faster first steps; fine-tuning is added if they are insufficient.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Training a new foundation model from scratch: Training from scratch is far too costly.
• Deleting the labeled data and using defaults: Discarding data wastes an asset.
• Continued pre-training on the small labeled set: Continued pre-training needs large unlabeled data.

Key takeaway: Try prompting and RAG before fine-tuning.

stem: A team trains a smaller model to imitate the outputs of a larger model so it runs cheaper at inference. What is this technique called?

choices.text: Model distillation
Transfer learning
Data poisoning
Prompt chaining

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Distillation trains a smaller student model to reproduce a larger teacher model's behavior, reducing inference cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer learning: Transfer learning reuses a trained model for a new task.
• Data poisoning: Data poisoning is an attack.
• Prompt chaining: Prompt chaining splits tasks across prompts.

Key takeaway: Distillation makes smaller models imitate larger ones.

stem: Which TWO data characteristics matter most when preparing a fine-tuning dataset? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Examples match the format and task of the target use
Sensitive personal data is kept in so the model learns it
Data is gathered from as many unrelated domains as possible
Every example is duplicated several times for emphasis
Labels and responses are accurate and consistent

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Relevant, correctly formatted, accurate, and consistent examples produce effective fine-tuning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Sensitive personal data is kept in so the…: Sensitive data should be removed.
• Data is gathered from as many unrelated…: Unrelated data dilutes learning.
• Every example is duplicated several times…: Duplicates skew training.

Key takeaway: Fine-tuning data must be relevant, accurate, and consistent.

stem: A team evaluates a translation model by comparing its output with reference translations. Which metric is commonly used?

choices.text: RMSE
MAPE
Recall
BLEU

explanation:
Why this is correct:
BLEU measures overlap between machine translations and reference translations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RMSE: RMSE measures regression error.
• MAPE: MAPE measures percentage forecast error.
• Recall: Recall is a classification metric.

Key takeaway: BLEU for translation; ROUGE for summarization.

stem: A company wants to evaluate open-ended chatbot answers at scale where no single reference answer exists. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Use only exact string matching against one reference answer per question
Use a model as a judge with a clear scoring rubric, spot-checked by humans
Measure response length and treat longer answers as more correct
Count how many times the chatbot uses the company's product names

explanation:
Why this is correct:
LLM-as-a-judge scores open-ended responses against a rubric at scale, with human spot checks to validate the judge.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use only exact string matching against one…: Exact match fails for varied wording.
• Measure response length and treat longer…: Length is not correctness.
• Count how many times the chatbot uses the…: Keyword counts are not quality.

Key takeaway: Evaluate open-ended outputs with rubric-based judging plus human checks.

stem: Before choosing a model, a team wants to see how candidate models perform on its own sample tasks. Which approach is most informative?

choices.text: Choose the model with the largest number of parameters available
Choose the model with the highest score on a public leaderboard
Evaluate candidates on a representative set of the company's tasks
Choose the model that was released most recently by any vendor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Public benchmarks may not reflect a company's tasks; testing candidates on representative internal examples is more informative.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Choose the model with the largest number of…: Size does not guarantee fit.
• Choose the model with the highest score on a…: Leaderboards may not match the use case.
• Choose the model that was released most…: Newness does not guarantee fit.

Key takeaway: Evaluate models on your own representative tasks.

stem: A model predicts whether a transaction is fraudulent or legitimate. Which task type is this?

choices.text: Topic modeling
Dimensionality reduction
Binary classification
Linear regression

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Predicting one of two classes is binary classification.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Topic modeling: Topic modeling finds themes in text.
• Dimensionality reduction: Dimensionality reduction compresses features.
• Linear regression: Regression predicts continuous values.

Key takeaway: Two classes → binary classification.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes deep learning from traditional machine learning?

choices.text: Deep learning never needs data, while traditional machine learning always does
Deep learning is limited to tabular data, while traditional ML handles images
Traditional machine learning runs only on GPUs, while deep learning runs on CPUs
Deep learning uses multi-layer neural networks that learn features automatically

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deep learning uses multi-layer neural networks that learn representations from raw data, excelling on images, audio, and text.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deep learning never needs data, while…: Deep learning typically needs large amounts of data.
• Deep learning is limited to tabular data,…: Deep learning excels on unstructured data.
• Traditional machine learning runs only on…: Hardware needs are generally the reverse.

Key takeaway: Deep learning = multi-layer neural networks with learned features.

stem: A fraud model flags 100 transactions, of which 80 are actually fraudulent. Which metric does 80% represent?

choices.text: Precision
Recall
R-squared
Specificity

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Precision is the share of flagged cases that are truly positive: 80 of 100.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Recall: Recall is the share of actual fraud that was caught.
• R-squared: R-squared is a regression metric.
• Specificity: Specificity concerns correctly identified negatives.

Key takeaway: Precision = correct among flagged; recall = caught among actual.

stem: A data scientist describes 'labeled data' for a spam filter. What does this mean?

choices.text: Emails stored in a compressed file format
Emails already marked as spam or not spam
Emails with personal names removed first
Emails sorted into folders by sending date

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Labeled data includes the known outcome (spam or not) that a supervised model learns to predict.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Emails stored in a compressed file format: Compression is storage, not labels.
• Emails with personal names removed first: Removing names is anonymization.
• Emails sorted into folders by sending date: Date sorting is not a label for the task.

Key takeaway: Labels are the known outcomes supervised models learn from.

stem: A company wants to forecast product demand for the next 12 weeks from historical sales. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A text summarization model
A speech recognition model
A time-series forecasting model
An image classification model

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Predicting future values from historical sequences is time-series forecasting; SageMaker AI and other tools support it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A text summarization model: Summarization condenses text.
• A speech recognition model: Speech recognition converts audio to text.
• An image classification model: Image models classify pictures.

Key takeaway: Future values from history → time-series forecasting.

stem: A bank wants to spot unusual account activity patterns it has never seen before, with few labeled fraud cases. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Supervised classification of known fraud types
Anomaly detection that learns normal behavior
Machine translation of transaction descriptions
Text-to-speech alerts for every transaction made

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Anomaly detection flags deviations from normal behavior and works when labeled examples of new fraud are scarce.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Supervised classification of known fraud types: Supervised models need labeled examples of the patterns.
• Machine translation of transaction descriptions: Translation does not detect anomalies.
• Text-to-speech alerts for every transaction made: Speech alerts do not detect anything.

Key takeaway: Few labels and novel patterns → anomaly detection.

stem: A company wants to transcribe customer calls and identify frequently mentioned issues. Which combination of AWS services fits?

choices.text: Amazon Polly followed by Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Translate followed by Amazon Lex
Amazon Textract followed by Amazon Forecast
Amazon Transcribe followed by Amazon Comprehend

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transcribe converts speech to text, and Comprehend extracts key phrases and topics from that text.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Polly followed by Amazon Rekognition: Polly generates speech; Rekognition analyzes images.
• Amazon Translate followed by Amazon Lex: Translate converts languages; Lex builds bots.
• Amazon Textract followed by Amazon Forecast: Textract reads documents; Forecast predicts time series.

Key takeaway: Speech-to-text then NLP: Transcribe + Comprehend.

stem: An e-commerce site wants real-time product recommendations based on each user's behavior without building models. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Personalize
Amazon Kendra
AWS Glue DataBrew
Amazon Lookout for Vision

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Personalize provides managed, real-time recommendations trained on user interaction data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Kendra: Kendra is enterprise search.
• AWS Glue DataBrew: DataBrew prepares data.
• Amazon Lookout for Vision: Lookout for Vision detects visual defects.

Key takeaway: Managed recommendations → Amazon Personalize.

stem: A team needs thousands of images labeled by human workers to train a model. Which AWS service helps manage this?

choices.text: Amazon SageMaker Clarify
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
Amazon SageMaker Neo

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Ground Truth manages data labeling workflows with human workers and can use automated labeling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SageMaker Clarify: Clarify detects bias.
• Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor: Model Monitor watches deployed models.
• Amazon SageMaker Neo: Neo optimizes models for hardware.

Key takeaway: Data labeling → SageMaker Ground Truth.

stem: A team wants to find the best learning rate and tree depth for a model automatically. Which technique does this describe?

choices.text: Data augmentation
Model deployment
Feature engineering
Hyperparameter tuning

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Hyperparameter tuning searches for the configuration values that give the best model performance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data augmentation: Data augmentation expands the dataset.
• Model deployment: Deployment serves the trained model.
• Feature engineering: Feature engineering creates input variables.

Key takeaway: Searching training settings = hyperparameter tuning.

stem: A company needs predictions on 10 million records once a week and does not need real-time responses. Which inference approach fits?

choices.text: Batch transform or batch inference
A real-time endpoint kept running
Serverless inference per request
Edge inference on user devices

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Batch inference processes large datasets on a schedule without keeping endpoints running, which is cost-effective for offline work.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A real-time endpoint kept running: Real-time endpoints cost more for periodic bulk jobs.
• Serverless inference per request: Per-request serverless is designed for intermittent real-time calls.
• Edge inference on user devices: Edge inference runs on devices, not for bulk weekly jobs.

Key takeaway: Large periodic jobs → batch inference.

stem: Which step of the ML lifecycle involves creating new input variables, such as 'days since last purchase,' from raw data?

choices.text: Model monitoring
Model deployment
Feature engineering
Hyperparameter tuning

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Feature engineering transforms raw data into informative inputs for a model.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Model monitoring: Monitoring watches production behavior.
• Model deployment: Deployment serves the model.
• Hyperparameter tuning: Tuning adjusts training settings.

Key takeaway: Creating model inputs = feature engineering.

stem: Which TWO signs indicate a model is underfitting? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Poor accuracy on validation data as well
Accuracy that improves only on test data
Near-perfect accuracy on the training data
Large gap between training and test accuracy
Poor accuracy on the training data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Underfitting means the model is too simple to capture patterns, so it performs poorly on both training and validation data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Accuracy that improves only on test data: That pattern is not typical of underfitting.
• Near-perfect accuracy on the training data: Near-perfect training accuracy suggests overfitting.
• Large gap between training and test accuracy: A large gap indicates overfitting.

Key takeaway: Underfitting = poor on both training and validation data.

stem: A company is reviewing a list of proposed automation projects. Which TWO situations are good fits for AI/ML? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Adding two numbers in a spreadsheet column
Calculating sales tax with a fixed legal formula
Detecting defects from images on a production line
Sorting a list of names in alphabetical order
Predicting customer churn from usage history

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Visual defect detection and churn prediction involve complex patterns; fixed formulas and sorting are deterministic tasks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Adding two numbers in a spreadsheet column: Arithmetic is deterministic.
• Calculating sales tax with a fixed legal formula: Fixed formulas suit deterministic code.
• Sorting a list of names in alphabetical order: Sorting is a simple algorithm.

Key takeaway: Use ML for complex patterns, not fixed rules.

stem: A company wants to reuse the same engineered features across training and real-time inference to avoid inconsistency. Which SageMaker capability fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Ground Truth
SageMaker Debugger
SageMaker Studio Lab
SageMaker Feature Store

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Feature Store keeps features consistent between training (offline) and inference (online).

Why the other options are wrong:
• SageMaker Ground Truth: Ground Truth labels data.
• SageMaker Debugger: Debugger monitors training.
• SageMaker Studio Lab: Studio Lab is a free learning environment.

Key takeaway: Consistent features for training and inference → Feature Store.

stem: A model predicts a customer's likelihood to buy as 0.73. Which statement about this output is correct?

choices.text: It means 73% of the model's training data came from this customer
It is a probability score that can be compared with a threshold
It guarantees the customer will buy within the next 73 days
It shows the model's training is 73% complete for this customer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Many models output probabilities; a business sets a threshold to decide actions based on the score.

Why the other options are wrong:
• It means 73% of the model's training data…: It says nothing about training data composition.
• It guarantees the customer will buy within…: A probability is not a guarantee or timeframe.
• It shows the model's training is 73%…: It is not training progress.

Key takeaway: Model scores are probabilities used with thresholds.

stem: A manufacturer wants to detect defects in product images using a managed service with few labeled examples. Which AWS option fits?

choices.text: Amazon Translate Custom Terminology
Amazon Comprehend Custom Entities
Amazon Transcribe Custom Vocabulary
Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Rekognition Custom Labels trains image classification or detection models from relatively few labeled images.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Translate Custom Terminology: Translate works on language translation.
• Amazon Comprehend Custom Entities: Comprehend works on text.
• Amazon Transcribe Custom Vocabulary: Transcribe works on audio.

Key takeaway: Custom image detection with few labels → Rekognition Custom Labels.

stem: A team describes a model that was trained on large amounts of text to predict the next word and can then answer questions, summarize, and translate. What type of model is this?

choices.text: A k-nearest neighbors model
A decision tree model
A large language model
A linear regression model

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Large language models are trained on large text corpora to predict tokens, enabling many language tasks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A k-nearest neighbors model: KNN classifies by similarity to labeled examples.
• A decision tree model: Decision trees classify tabular data.
• A linear regression model: Linear regression predicts numeric values.

Key takeaway: Broad language tasks from next-token training = LLM.

stem: A team wants a chatbot to stop generating text as soon as it outputs the marker 'END'. Which inference setting fits?

choices.text: A seed value
A stop sequence
A temperature
A top-k value

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Stop sequences tell the model to end generation when a specific string appears.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A seed value: A seed affects reproducibility where supported.
• A temperature: Temperature controls randomness.
• A top-k value: Top-k limits candidate tokens.

Key takeaway: End output at a marker with stop sequences.

stem: Which statement about generative adversarial networks (GANs) is accurate?

choices.text: A generator creates samples while a discriminator learns to tell real from fake
A model predicts numeric values from tabular features using trees
Two networks translate text between languages in opposite directions
A single network memorizes training images and returns the closest one

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GANs train a generator and discriminator against each other, improving the realism of generated samples.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A model predicts numeric values from tabular…: That describes tree-based regression.
• Two networks translate text between…: That describes translation models.
• A single network memorizes training images…: GANs generate new samples rather than retrieving stored ones.

Key takeaway: GANs pit a generator against a discriminator.

stem: A company wants to use generative AI to summarize long internal reports for executives. Which benefit is most realistic?

choices.text: Complete removal of the need to ever read the original reports
Perfect accuracy on every figure without any review by the team
Faster review of key points, with humans checking important details
Guaranteed legal approval of each summary before distribution

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Summaries speed up review, but important details should still be checked against the source.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Complete removal of the need to ever read…: Originals remain the source of truth.
• Perfect accuracy on every figure without any…: Summaries can contain errors.
• Guaranteed legal approval of each summary…: No legal guarantee exists.

Key takeaway: GenAI summaries save time; verify important details.

stem: A company plans to use a foundation model to generate personalized emails to millions of customers. Which TWO risks should it plan for? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The model refusing to generate any text in English
The emails being delivered only to customers in one Region
The model permanently storing each customer's email address
Incorrect or inappropriate content reaching customers at scale
Inference costs growing with message volume and length

explanation:
Why this is correct:
At scale, content errors multiply and token-based costs rise with volume; review processes and cost controls are needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The model refusing to generate any text in…: Models generate English text.
• The emails being delivered only to customers…: Delivery is unrelated to the model.
• The model permanently storing each…: Managed models do not store inputs for training by default on Bedrock.

Key takeaway: At scale, plan for content quality and cost.

stem: A company wants to try out Bedrock models interactively in the console before writing code. Which feature fits?

choices.text: The Route 53 console
The Bedrock playgrounds
The IAM access analyzer
The AWS CLI profile

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock playgrounds let users test prompts and models interactively in the console.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The Route 53 console: Route 53 manages DNS.
• The IAM access analyzer: Access Analyzer reviews permissions.
• The AWS CLI profile: The CLI requires commands and is not interactive testing of models.

Key takeaway: Try models interactively in Bedrock playgrounds.

stem: A company must train a very large model and wants AWS hardware designed to lower training cost. Which option fits?

choices.text: AWS Trainium instances
AWS Wavelength Zones
AWS Inferentia chips
AWS Snowball devices

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Trainium is purpose-built for cost-effective deep learning training; Inferentia targets inference.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Wavelength Zones: Wavelength provides edge compute in 5G networks.
• AWS Inferentia chips: Inferentia is optimized for inference.
• AWS Snowball devices: Snowball transfers data physically.

Key takeaway: Training → Trainium; inference → Inferentia.

stem: An agent must remember a user's preferences across separate sessions. Which design element supports this?

choices.text: A higher temperature in each new session
A new model version every single session
A longer max token limit for each reply
Persistent memory stored outside the model

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Models do not retain state between sessions; persistent memory, such as AgentCore Memory, stores and retrieves preferences.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A higher temperature in each new session: Temperature affects randomness.
• A new model version every single session: Changing models does not add memory.
• A longer max token limit for each reply: Output length does not create memory.

Key takeaway: Cross-session memory must be stored outside the model.

stem: A company's RAG system must answer in under one second at high volume. Which TWO design choices help most? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Retrieve fewer, more relevant chunks per question
Chain five separate models for every single answer
Send every document in the corpus with each prompt
Raise max output tokens to the highest allowed value
Use a smaller, faster model that meets quality needs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Smaller models reduce generation latency, and fewer, better chunks reduce prompt size and processing time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Chain five separate models for every single…: Chaining many models adds latency.
• Send every document in the corpus with each…: Sending the corpus is slow and costly.
• Raise max output tokens to the highest…: Longer outputs increase latency.

Key takeaway: For low latency, right-size the model and trim retrieved context.

stem: In a RAG pipeline, what happens during the 'retrieval' step?

choices.text: The model's weights are updated with new documents
The user's account permissions are reset for access
Relevant passages are found and added to the prompt
The final answer is translated into another language

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Retrieval searches the knowledge store for relevant passages and supplies them to the model as context.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The model's weights are updated with new…: RAG does not update weights.
• The user's account permissions are reset for…: Permissions are not reset.
• The final answer is translated into another…: Translation is unrelated.

Key takeaway: Retrieval supplies relevant context to the prompt.

stem: A prompt keeps producing long answers when the team wants three bullet points. Which prompt change helps most?

choices.text: Increase the temperature so the model explores other formats
State the exact format and length required in the prompt
Ask the model to produce as many bullet points as it can
Remove all instructions and let the model decide the format

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Explicit format and length instructions guide the model to the desired output shape.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Increase the temperature so the model…: Temperature adds randomness, not format control.
• Ask the model to produce as many bullet…: That encourages longer output.
• Remove all instructions and let the model…: Removing instructions worsens control.

Key takeaway: State format and length explicitly.

stem: A company wants its prompts to resist users who try to override instructions. Which TWO practices help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Remove all instructions from the system prompt
Let user input overwrite the system prompt freely
Apply guardrails that detect prompt attacks
Tell users the full system prompt in the interface
Separate system instructions from user input clearly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clear separation of instructions from input and automated prompt-attack detection reduce injection success.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove all instructions from the system prompt: Without instructions, behavior is uncontrolled.
• Let user input overwrite the system prompt…: Allowing overwrites enables injection.
• Tell users the full system prompt in the…: Revealing the system prompt helps attackers.

Key takeaway: Separate instructions from input and filter prompt attacks.

stem: A prompt contains placeholders such as {customer_name} that are filled in by the application. What is this pattern called?

choices.text: A prompt template
A model checkpoint
A stop sequence
A vector index

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Prompt templates contain reusable instructions with variables filled at runtime.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A model checkpoint: Checkpoints save model training state.
• A stop sequence: Stop sequences end generation.
• A vector index: Vector indexes store embeddings.

Key takeaway: Reusable prompts with variables = prompt templates.

stem: Which statement about fine-tuning versus in-context learning is correct?

choices.text: In-context learning permanently changes weights; fine-tuning only edits prompts
Neither technique can change how a model responds to a given task at all
Both techniques require training a new model from scratch on company data
Fine-tuning changes model weights; in-context learning uses examples in the prompt

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fine-tuning updates weights with training data; in-context learning guides behavior through examples in the prompt without training.

Why the other options are wrong:
• In-context learning permanently changes…: The descriptions are reversed.
• Neither technique can change how a model…: Both can change task behavior.
• Both techniques require training a new model…: Neither trains from scratch.

Key takeaway: Fine-tuning changes weights; in-context learning uses prompts.

stem: A company fine-tuned a model, and it now performs worse on general tasks it previously handled well. What is this effect called?

choices.text: Prompt injection risk
Catastrophic forgetting
Positive transfer gain
Retrieval grounding

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fine-tuning on narrow data can cause a model to lose some general capabilities, known as catastrophic forgetting.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Prompt injection risk: Prompt injection is an input attack.
• Positive transfer gain: Positive transfer would improve performance.
• Retrieval grounding: Grounding is a RAG concept.

Key takeaway: Narrow fine-tuning can cause catastrophic forgetting.

stem: A team wants to measure whether a RAG system retrieves the right passages for each question. Which evaluation focus fits?

choices.text: Retrieval relevance of returned passages
Grammar quality of the final answers
Average length of the final answers
Number of documents in the source bucket

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Retrieval relevance checks whether the passages returned actually address the question, which drives answer quality.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Grammar quality of the final answers: Grammar does not measure retrieval.
• Average length of the final answers: Length does not measure retrieval.
• Number of documents in the source bucket: Document count does not measure relevance.

Key takeaway: Evaluate RAG retrieval relevance separately from generation.

stem: Which TWO evaluation practices give the most reliable view of a generative AI application's quality? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Test only on the examples used in the prompt
Evaluate once before launch and never again
Rely on a single metric such as response length
Combine automatic metrics with human review
Test on a representative set of real use cases

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Representative test sets and a mix of automated and human evaluation give a trustworthy picture of quality.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Test only on the examples used in the prompt: Prompt examples overstate quality.
• Evaluate once before launch and never again: Quality can change after launch.
• Rely on a single metric such as response length: One metric misses dimensions.

Key takeaway: Evaluate on representative data with automatic and human methods.

stem: A company wants its chatbot to respond in the user's language across 20 languages. Which model selection factor is most important?

choices.text: Number of parameters, regardless of language support
Multilingual capability in the needed languages
Release date of the newest version of the model
Maximum image resolution the model can generate

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The model must perform well in each required language; testing on real samples in those languages confirms it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Number of parameters, regardless of language…: Size does not guarantee language coverage.
• Release date of the newest version of the model: Newness does not guarantee language support.
• Maximum image resolution the model can generate: Image resolution is unrelated.

Key takeaway: Choose models by the capabilities your use case needs.

stem: A company wants an AI agent to complete tasks across several internal systems with multiple steps. Which TWO capabilities are essential? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A larger image generation model for each system
A higher temperature for more creative task steps
Controls that limit and log what actions it may take
Removal of all instructions to maximize flexibility
The ability to call tools or APIs for each system

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Agents act through tools, and they need permissions, limits, and logging to act safely.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A larger image generation model for each system: Image generation is unrelated.
• A higher temperature for more creative task…: Creativity is not needed for task execution.
• Removal of all instructions to maximize…: Removing instructions reduces reliability.

Key takeaway: Agents need tools plus action limits and logs.

stem: A team wants to test several prompt variations to see which produces the best results for the same task. Which practice fits?

choices.text: Pick the prompt that uses the most technical vocabulary
Pick the prompt written most recently by any team member
Pick the longest prompt, since longer prompts are always better
Compare the variants on the same test inputs and measure outcomes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Systematic comparison on the same inputs with defined metrics identifies the best-performing prompt.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pick the prompt that uses the most technical…: Technical vocabulary does not guarantee quality.
• Pick the prompt written most recently by any…: Recency does not guarantee quality.
• Pick the longest prompt, since longer…: Length does not guarantee quality.

Key takeaway: Evaluate prompt variants on the same test set.

stem: A company wants to encrypt its fine-tuning data and custom models in Amazon Bedrock with keys it controls. Which service provides these keys?

choices.text: AWS Key Management Service
AWS Directory Service
AWS Certificate Manager
AWS Secrets Manager

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock supports customer managed keys in AWS KMS for encrypting customization data and custom models.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Directory Service: Directory Service provides managed Active Directory.
• AWS Certificate Manager: ACM manages TLS certificates.
• AWS Secrets Manager: Secrets Manager stores credentials.

Key takeaway: Customer-controlled encryption keys → AWS KMS.

stem: A company wants to detect suspicious activity such as unusual API calls in accounts running AI workloads. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Detective
Amazon GuardDuty
Amazon Lex V2
AWS Glue DataBrew

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty continuously monitors accounts for threats, including anomalous API activity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Detective: Detective helps investigate findings after they are detected; it is not the continuous threat detector.
• Amazon Lex V2: Lex builds bots.
• AWS Glue DataBrew: DataBrew prepares data.

Key takeaway: Threat detection across accounts → Amazon GuardDuty.

stem: A company wants to scan the container images and EC2 instances hosting its ML models for software vulnerabilities. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Shield Advanced
Amazon Macie
Amazon Inspector
AWS Artifact

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inspector scans EC2 instances, container images, and Lambda functions for known vulnerabilities.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Shield Advanced: Shield protects against DDoS.
• Amazon Macie: Macie finds sensitive data in S3.
• AWS Artifact: Artifact provides compliance documents.

Key takeaway: Vulnerability scanning → Amazon Inspector.

stem: Which TWO controls reduce the risk of leaking sensitive data through a generative AI application? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Grant the app administrator access to all data stores
Log prompts to a publicly readable storage bucket
Apply least-privilege access to data sources the app can use
Share one set of credentials among all application users
Filter or mask personal data in inputs and outputs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Least privilege limits what the app can reach, and PII filtering prevents exposure in prompts and responses.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Grant the app administrator access to all…: Broad access increases exposure.
• Log prompts to a publicly readable storage…: Public logs leak data.
• Share one set of credentials among all…: Shared credentials remove accountability.

Key takeaway: Limit access and filter sensitive data.

stem: A company wants the prompts it sends to Amazon Bedrock to not be used to train the providers' base models. What is true about Bedrock by default?

choices.text: Customer prompts and outputs are not used to train the base models
Prompts are published publicly unless a support case is opened
Every prompt is shared with all model providers to improve the models
Customers must pay extra to prevent prompts from being used in training

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon Bedrock does not use customer inputs and outputs to train the underlying foundation models by default.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Prompts are published publicly unless a…: Prompts are not published.
• Every prompt is shared with all model…: Prompts are not shared for training.
• Customers must pay extra to prevent prompts…: No extra fee is needed.

Key takeaway: Bedrock does not use your data to train base models.

stem: A company must produce audit-ready evidence of its AWS controls for an AI compliance review. Which service helps automate evidence collection?

choices.text: Amazon CloudFront
Amazon Polly
AWS Batch
AWS Audit Manager

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Audit Manager continuously collects evidence from AWS usage to help prepare for audits against frameworks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon CloudFront: CloudFront delivers content.
• Amazon Polly: Polly synthesizes speech.
• AWS Batch: Batch runs batch computing jobs.

Key takeaway: Automated audit evidence → AWS Audit Manager.

stem: A company wants to check its AWS environment against best practices, including security and cost, for its AI workloads. Which service provides recommendations?

choices.text: Amazon Kendra
AWS Trusted Advisor
Amazon Comprehend
AWS Transfer Family

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trusted Advisor inspects the environment and recommends improvements for security, cost, performance, and fault tolerance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Kendra: Kendra is search.
• Amazon Comprehend: Comprehend is NLP.
• AWS Transfer Family: Transfer Family provides SFTP and similar transfers.

Key takeaway: Best-practice recommendations → AWS Trusted Advisor.

stem: A company must show which data sources were used to train a model and how that data was transformed. Which governance concept is this?

choices.text: Data striping
Data caching
Data lineage
Data sharding

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data lineage traces data from its sources through transformations, supporting audits and accountability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data striping: Striping spreads data across disks.
• Data caching: Caching speeds access.
• Data sharding: Sharding splits data for scale.

Key takeaway: Tracing data origins and transformations = data lineage.

stem: Which TWO practices support governance of generative AI in an organization? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Allow each employee to choose any public AI tool freely
Define policies for acceptable use and review of AI outputs
Delete logs frequently to minimize stored information
Avoid documenting models to reduce administrative work
Maintain an inventory of AI applications and their owners

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An inventory with owners and clear usage and review policies provide the visibility and rules governance needs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Allow each employee to choose any public AI…: Unmanaged tool use creates risk.
• Delete logs frequently to minimize stored…: Logs support audits.
• Avoid documenting models to reduce…: Documentation is needed for oversight.

Key takeaway: Govern GenAI with inventories and usage policies.

stem: A company must retain records of AI model decisions for five years to meet regulations, then delete them automatically. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Keep records only in application memory until the servers restart
Email the records to the compliance team each day for manual storage
Store records on developer laptops and delete them when convenient
Store records in S3 with lifecycle rules for retention and expiration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 lifecycle policies can transition and expire objects automatically, meeting retention requirements reliably.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keep records only in application memory…: Memory is lost on restart.
• Email the records to the compliance team…: Email is not a reliable record store.
• Store records on developer laptops and…: Laptops are not governed storage.

Key takeaway: Automate retention and deletion with S3 lifecycle rules.

stem: A company wants to give a Lambda function that calls Bedrock only the permissions it needs. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Attach an IAM role with a policy limited to the required actions
Give the function the root account credentials for simplicity
Embed an administrator's access keys in the function's code
Store a shared password in an environment variable for all apps

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An execution role with least-privilege permissions provides temporary credentials and limits what the function can do.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Give the function the root account…: Root credentials must never be used this way.
• Embed an administrator's access keys in the…: Embedded keys are risky and over-privileged.
• Store a shared password in an environment…: Shared passwords are insecure.

Key takeaway: Use least-privilege IAM roles for workloads.

stem: A company asks which AWS framework helps it design secure, reliable, and efficient AI workloads using best practices. Which framework fits?

choices.text: The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework
The AWS Well-Architected Framework
The AWS Service Catalog
The AWS Pricing Calculator

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Well-Architected Framework provides best practices across pillars such as security, reliability, and cost; lenses such as the Generative AI Lens extend it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework: The CAF guides organizational cloud adoption.
• The AWS Service Catalog: Service Catalog manages approved products.
• The AWS Pricing Calculator: The Pricing Calculator estimates costs.

Key takeaway: Workload best practices → Well-Architected Framework and lenses.

stem: A company's AI app retrieves documents from S3. It wants only this app's role to read the bucket. Which control enforces this at the bucket level?

choices.text: An S3 event notification that triggers on each upload
An S3 lifecycle rule that archives objects after a day
An S3 storage class change to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
An S3 bucket policy allowing only the app's IAM role

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bucket policies can restrict access to specific principals, such as the application's role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An S3 event notification that triggers on…: Event notifications trigger workflows.
• An S3 lifecycle rule that archives objects…: Lifecycle rules manage storage transitions.
• An S3 storage class change to S3 Glacier…: Storage classes affect cost and retrieval time.

Key takeaway: Restrict bucket access with bucket policies.

stem: A company operating under a regulated framework wants AI workloads deployed only through pre-approved, compliant templates. Which AWS service helps?

choices.text: AWS Service Catalog
Amazon Personalize
AWS Elemental
Amazon Kinesis

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Service Catalog lets organizations offer approved templates so teams deploy only compliant configurations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Personalize: Personalize provides recommendations.
• AWS Elemental: Elemental processes media.
• Amazon Kinesis: Kinesis streams data.

Key takeaway: Enforce approved deployments with AWS Service Catalog.

stem: A company wants human reviewers to check a sample of an AI model's content moderation decisions. Which practice does this support?

choices.text: Data sharding to speed up storage access
Model distillation to reduce inference costs
Human oversight to catch and correct model errors
Token caching to reduce response latency

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sampling decisions for human review provides oversight and feedback to improve the system.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data sharding to speed up storage access: Sharding is a storage technique.
• Model distillation to reduce inference costs: Distillation reduces cost.
• Token caching to reduce response latency: Caching reduces latency.

Key takeaway: Human review provides oversight of AI decisions.

stem: A company wants to reduce toxic outputs from a generative AI model before launch. Which TWO actions help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Raise temperature to make outputs less predictable
Test the model with adversarial prompts before launch
Remove all system instructions to simplify prompts
Skip testing and rely on user complaints after launch
Configure content filters for harmful categories

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Red-teaming with adversarial prompts finds weaknesses, and content filters block harmful outputs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Raise temperature to make outputs less…: Randomness can increase harmful outputs.
